---
title: "Activity: campus café sales"
subtitle: "Turn a year of register data into a dashboard the café manager can trust. About 45 minutes, plus 10 to make it yours."
---

You help run a campus café. The manager wants a one-page dashboard: how sales moved over the year, what sells best,
and whether exam weeks really are as busy as they feel. You have a year of the register's daily sales, and you have
Claude Code.

You'll go around the agent loop once: **read → plan → act → check**. Then you'll make the result stick with memory
and a skill, undo a bad change, and share what you built. The data is synthetic.

::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Your finish line

You're done when you have all of these:

- `dashboard.html` opens in your browser and compares exam weeks, **using the café's real exam dates**
- Its fall-semester total matches the **official figure**
- `CLAUDE.md` holds what you learned, and Claude uses it after `/clear`
- `/house-style` gives a page the NC State look
- You have a link to share (Pro plan or higher), or a screenshot
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Working as a pair?

The **checker** holds two things: the note from the café manager (step 2) and the official figure (step 4). Read the plan
against the note before anyone approves it, and compare the dashboard's number with the official one.
:::

## Before you start

1. Install Claude Code and sign in: see [Set up](../setup.qmd).
2. Download [cafe.zip](../downloads/cafe.zip) and unzip it to your Desktop. On a Mac, double-click it and drag the
   `cafe` folder it makes to your Desktop. On Windows, right-click it, choose **Extract All**, then **Extract**, and
   drag the `cafe` folder to your Desktop. The folder holds `README.md` and `cafe_sales.csv`.
3. Open a terminal, go into the folder, and start Claude Code:

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Mac

::: {.prompt .prompt-shell}
```bash
cd ~/Desktop/cafe
claude
```
:::

### Windows

::: {.prompt .prompt-shell}
```powershell
cd $HOME\Desktop\cafe
claude
```
:::

If PowerShell says the path doesn't exist, your Desktop is probably in OneDrive: try `cd $HOME\OneDrive\Desktop\cafe`.
:::

Folder not found, on either system? Type `cd` and a space, drag the `cafe` folder from Finder or File
Explorer onto the terminal window, and press {{< kbd Enter >}}. Then type `claude`.

4. Claude Code asks for a quick safety check: is this a project you trust? It is: it holds only what you just
   unzipped. Choose **Yes, I trust this folder** (use the arrow keys if it isn't highlighted) and press
   {{< kbd Enter >}}. If Claude Code closes instead, that was **No, exit**: run `claude` again.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Work in this folder only

Claude Code can read and change everything in the folder you start it in. Starting it in your home folder or
Desktop gives it far more reach than this task needs.
:::

## <span class="step-badge">1</span> Read

Ask what's there before asking for anything else.

::: {.prompt}
```default
What's in this folder? Give me a quick summary of the data. Don't change anything yet.
```
:::

::: {.watch}
Claude opens the files itself. A chatbot would have asked you to paste them in. Each step shows as a line: the files it
read, and commands it ran, like `Bash(wc -l cafe_sales.csv)`. {{< kbd Ctrl-O >}} shows the details.
:::

Read its summary closely. It will likely point out oddities: days with no sales at all, an item whose name changes,
a price that doesn't look right. **Decide what you think about each one**; you'll see them again in the plan.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## What happened in our rehearsal

Claude read both files and flagged four things before being asked: "Cold Brew" renamed to "Cold Brew Coffee" on Jan 7;
three price increases the same day; **one latte rung up at $45.00** (*"probably a decimal slip"*); and **33 days with
zero sales for every item**, which it suspected were closures.
:::

## <span class="step-badge">2</span> Plan

The manager sent you this note this morning:

::: {.note-card}
<span class="note-from">From the café manager</span>

Exam weeks this year were **Oct 6–10** and **Dec 8–16** in the fall, and **Mar 2–6** and **Apr 28–May 7** in the
spring. We were closed over the breaks, so those days show zero sales.
:::

Claude can't see the note, and the prompt below doesn't mention it. That's on purpose. **Predict first:** will
Claude ask you for the exam dates, or work them out some other way?

::: {.prompt}
```default
/plan Build a one-page dashboard, dashboard.html, for the café manager: daily sales across the year, the best-selling items, and whether exam weeks are busier. Make it a single file I can open by double-clicking.
```
:::

The mode line at the bottom now reads `⏸ plan mode on`. Claude explores, may ask you a question or two, then shows a
plan and asks how to proceed. **Don't approve it yet.**

- **If it asks for the exam dates:** answer from the note. If it shows choices, use the arrow keys and
  {{< kbd Enter >}}, or choose the option to type your own answer and paste the sentence below.
- **If it doesn't ask:** read the plan. How does it decide which weeks were exam weeks? If it plans to **guess them
  from the busiest weeks in the sales**, catch it. Two problems: the café's busiest weeks are a career fair and
  homecoming, not exams, and defining exam weeks by high sales would make "exam weeks are busier" true by definition.

To fix a wrong assumption before any code exists, choose **No, keep planning** (or answer its question), then type:

::: {.prompt}
```default
Exam weeks were Oct 6–10 and Dec 8–16 in the fall, and Mar 2–6 and Apr 28–May 7 in the spring. Use those exact dates, and leave days we were closed out of the averages.
```
:::

When the plan uses those dates, and handles the oddities from step 1 the way you want, choose
**Yes, manually approve edits**.

::: {.watch}
In our rehearsals Claude always asked for the exam dates, and it knew not to define them by the sales. But its
fallback, if you just said "go," was finals only (missing both midterm weeks) or no exam comparison at all.
In the default auto mode, Claude is built to keep working rather than stop for questions, so plan mode is where you
get to catch an assumption.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## What happened in our rehearsal

Claude asked for the exam dates, and said why it wouldn't infer them: *"picking the busiest weeks would make the answer
circular."* But its default, if not told, was **finals only** (Dec 8–16 and Apr 30–May 8), which misses both midterm
weeks. It also noted that sales "jump in early and late October, mid-February and early March, which might be
midterms": two of those were the career fair and homecoming. After the manager's dates, its plan compared each exam
week with ordinary days *of the same weekday in the same term*.
:::

## <span class="step-badge">3</span> Act

In manual mode, Claude asks before each change. Approve the first edit or two and look at what it's writing.

Then switch to auto mode and let it finish. The next time Claude asks to run a command, choose **Yes, and switch to
auto mode**. Or press {{< kbd Shift-Tab >}}, with no question on screen, until the mode line reads `⏵⏵ auto mode on`
(on Windows, if Shift+Tab does nothing, press {{< kbd Alt-M >}}). A separate safety check still reviews each action.
Press {{< kbd Esc >}} at any point to stop it and redirect.

The build can take 10 to 20 minutes: Claude writes the page, runs its code and checks its own numbers. That's normal.
**Wait for it to finish before you type the next prompt**: anything you type now reaches Claude mid-build.

When it's done, open the dashboard. Ask Claude to open it, or:

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Mac

::: {.prompt}
```default
! open dashboard.html
```
:::

### Windows

::: {.prompt}
```default
! start dashboard.html
```
:::
:::

The `!` runs a command yourself without leaving Claude Code. Double-clicking the file works too.

![A dashboard from a rehearsal run. Yours will look different: same prompt, different result.](../images/screens/cafe-dashboard.png){.shot fig-alt="A café dashboard from a rehearsal run: daily sales across the year, the best-selling items, and exam weeks compared with other weeks"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## What happened in our rehearsal

Claude pasted the CSV into the page with `cat`, confirmed the copy was identical, and ran the page's own calculation
code with macOS's built-in JavaScript runner to check its numbers: 43 checks, no failures. The page worked on the
first double-click. It reported exam days at **+18%** over ordinary days, and pointed out that the career fair and
homecoming weeks outsold every exam week. It also raised the weather as a confounder.
:::

## <span class="step-badge">4</span> Check

The manager already knows one number: what the café took in over the fall semester.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The official figure

::: {.answer}
<span class="answer-label">Official fall sales, Aug 18 – Dec 16, 2025</span><span class="answer-value">{{< var key.cafe.fall-total >}}</span>
:::

Does your dashboard agree? If it doesn't show a fall total, ask Claude for it.
:::

Whether it matches or not, make Claude prove it. `/goal` keeps Claude working until a condition holds, and a
separate model checks after every turn:

::: {.prompt}
```default
/goal The dashboard's fall-semester sales (Aug 18 to Dec 16, 2025) match the café's official $145,205.25. If they don't, explain why before changing anything. Prove the final number from the CSV yourself, and don't hard-code it. Stop after 5 turns.
```
:::

::: {.watch}
Why it might not match: one latte in September was rung up at $45.00. Did Claude flag it in step 1? Did the plan fix
it? A figure that's off by exactly the size of one typo is the kind of thing only a known answer catches.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## If your number doesn't match

A wrong number usually points straight at its cause:

| Your dashboard says | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **$145,205.25** | The $45.00 latte corrected to $4.50 ✓ |
| $148,769.25 | The $45.00 latte counted as rung up: $3,564 too high |
| $144,809.25 | The latte row dropped instead of corrected: $396 too low |
:::

If something on the page looks wrong, show Claude instead of describing it. Take a screenshot to the clipboard
({{< kbd mac=Ctrl-Shift-Cmd-4 >}} on a Mac, {{< kbd win=Win-Shift-S >}} on Windows), then paste it into your prompt
with {{< kbd Ctrl-V >}} (Mac Terminal) or {{< kbd Alt-V >}} (Windows) and say what's off.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## What happened in our rehearsal

The page didn't show a fall total, so `/goal` led Claude to add a **Totals by term** table: Fall 2025 =
**$145,205.25**, matching the official figure to the cent. It showed why the raw CSV says $148,769.25 instead: one
latte row priced $45.00, 88 sold, which is $3,564 too much. Its "not hard-coded" check even caught one of its own code
comments that contained the number, and removed it.
:::

## <span class="step-badge">5</span> Remember

Claude forgets everything when a conversation ends, except what's written down. Write what you learned in
`CLAUDE.md`, a file Claude reads at the start of every session in this folder.

::: {.prompt}
```default
Add what we learned to CLAUDE.md: the exam-week dates, that days with zero sales for every item mean we were closed, and that "Cold Brew Coffee" is the same item as "Cold Brew".
```
:::

Run `/memory` to see it listed, along with **auto memory**: notes Claude saves for itself as it works. `CLAUDE.md`
is what *you* tell it; auto memory is what *it* learns. Press {{< kbd Esc >}} to close the list; you don't need to
open anything.

Now test it. Type `/clear` to start a fresh conversation, then ask:

::: {.prompt}
```default
How much busier were exam weeks than other weeks, per day we were open?
```
:::

It should use your exam dates and skip the closed days without being told again.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## What happened in our rehearsal

Claude wrote a short `CLAUDE.md` with the exam dates, the closed-days rule and the Cold Brew rename, and asked whether
to add the latte fix and the January price rise too. A fresh session with only that file answered the exam-week
question using your dates and skipping closed days.
:::

## <span class="step-badge">6</span> Make a skill

A skill is a reusable set of instructions with a name. You run it as a command, and Claude can also use it on its own
when it fits. (Skills are what Claude Code used to call custom commands.) Have Claude write one:

::: {.prompt}
```default
Create a skill called house-style that gives any web page we make the NC State look: Wolfpack Red #CC0000 for highlights, dark gray text on white, Arial or Helvetica, a red header bar with the page title, and a footer that says "Synthetic data made for a workshop." Use it whenever you create or restyle a web page.
```
:::

Claude writes `.claude/skills/house-style/SKILL.md`. This folder had no skills before, so Claude Code isn't watching
that folder yet. Tell it to look once:

::: {.prompt}
```default
/reload-skills
```
:::

Then run your skill:

::: {.prompt}
```default
/house-style dashboard.html
```
:::

Reload the page in your browser. If Claude Code says **Unknown command: /house-style**, run `/reload-skills` and
try again. Change the skill later? Run `/reload-skills` again.

Now ask for something new, without mentioning the style, and watch whether Claude reaches for the skill on its own:

::: {.prompt}
```default
Make a flyer for the café, flyer.html, announcing longer hours during finals week.
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## What happened in our rehearsal

When the skill was first run, it wasn't found: the folder had no skills when the session started. That's why this
page tells you to run `/reload-skills`. For the flyer, Claude used the house style without
being asked. It didn't know the café's hours or which finals week was meant, so it left visible blanks,
`[opening time]` and `[closing time]`, rather than invent them.
:::

## <span class="step-badge">7</span> Undo

Everyone makes a change they regret. Make one on purpose:

::: {.prompt}
```default
Make dashboard.html rainbow-colored, with Comic Sans everywhere.
```
:::

Look at it. Then type `/rewind` (or press {{< kbd Esc >}} twice on an empty prompt), pick **your rainbow
prompt** itself, and choose **Restore code**. Rewind goes back to just before the prompt you pick. Reload: it's back.

::: {.callout-warning}
## What rewind can't undo

`/rewind` restores files Claude edited with its own editing tools. It **doesn't** undo what shell commands did, such
as deleting (`rm`) or moving (`mv`) files. For real work, keep copies or use git.
:::

## <span class="step-badge">8</span> Share

::: {.prompt}
```default
Publish dashboard.html as an artifact.
```
:::

Claude gives you a link to a private page on claude.ai. Open it, choose **Share**, and you can make a public link
anyone can open. This needs a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan. On a Team or Enterprise plan, public links are off
unless your organization turns them on, so share within your organization instead. On a Console account, share a
screenshot.
`/artifacts` lists what you've published.

## Make it yours

Ten minutes, one agent. Pick one:

- **Improve the dashboard:** a "sales vs. temperature" chart (do hot drinks sell more on cold days?), a dark mode, a
  print-friendly version for the manager.
- **Build something you'd use:** a study timer in NC State colors, a flashcard quiz from your own notes, a weekly
  planner. Start in a new empty folder: `/exit`, then `cd ..`, `mkdir my-project`, `cd my-project`
  and `claude`, the same on Mac and Windows.
- **Try your own data**, as long as it's data you're allowed to share with an AI service.

Give it a finish line Claude can prove from its own work, such as:

::: {.prompt}
```default
/goal every button on the page has code behind it that visibly changes the page, and the page needs no other files. Prove it from the code. Stop after 5 turns.
```
:::

## If something goes wrong

| What happens | Try |
| --- | --- |
| Claude asks a question instead of planning | Answer it. That's the plan step working. |
| The page opens blank | Paste a screenshot and say "this opens blank when I double-click it." |
| Your number doesn't match and you're stuck | Ask: "List every reason the fall total could differ from $145,205.25, and check each one." |
| A window offers to install "command line developer tools" (Mac) | Claude tried a tool your Mac doesn't have. Choose **Not Now**; it will find another way. |
| Claude has gone in circles twice | `/clear` and ask again, with what you learned in the first prompt. |
| Claude says "You've hit your Opus limit" | Type `/model sonnet` and carry on. |
| You're out of time | Download the [finished example](../downloads/cafe-finished.zip) and compare. |
